analysis.one_liner: Bans companies from forcing workers and consumers into arbitration instead of court.
analysis.headline: The House passed the FAIR Act 222-209 on March 17, 2022, but the Senate Judiciary Committee never acted on it and it died when the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Most people sign contracts—at hiring or when they buy something—that say any future dispute must go to a private arbitrator chosen by the company, not to a court, and that they cannot join a class action. The FAIR Act would make those pre-dispute clauses unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, letting people sue in court and band together in class actions. Companies could still offer arbitration voluntarily after a dispute actually arises.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, consumers, small businesses, and people facing discrimination, who regain the right to have their case heard by a judge or jury and to join class actions instead of being funneled into private arbitration where they typically face a company-chosen decision-maker, limited discovery, and little or no appeal.

how_it_helps.text: Makes predispute arbitration agreements and class-action waivers invalid and unenforceable for employment, consumer, antitrust, and civil rights disputes, and puts a court, not an arbitrator, in charge of deciding whether the law applies [S3][S5].
Covers independent contractors as well as employees, and protects the right to join class and collective actions, including wage cases under the Fair Labor Standards Act [S5].
Leaves voluntary arbitration intact: nothing prohibits parties from choosing arbitration after a dispute arises [S5].

analysis.who_pays: Employers, lenders, credit card issuers, and other companies that rely on pre-dispute arbitration clauses would lose their main shield against class-action litigation, facing more court cases, higher legal costs, and larger settlements, and the arbitration industry would lose its court-ordered volume of cases.

drawbacks.text: Businesses argue arbitration is faster and cheaper than court for individuals, and that pushing disputes into litigation raises legal costs that can be passed on through higher prices [S8] — House Republicans made this case in opposing the bill and offering a motion to recommit, which failed 208-222 [S7][S8].

Litigation is slow and expensive for a single plaintiff, and class actions deliver most of their value through attorneys' fees, so the bill trades a fast private forum for a court system many individuals cannot afford on their own.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is real and structural: without the ability to sue or join a class action, most people with small-dollar or discrimination claims effectively have no remedy, because companies can pick the forum, limit evidence, and appeal almost nothing. The cost is borne mainly by companies that drafted the arbitration clauses and by a private arbitration industry whose caseload would shrink. The strongest counterargument—that arbitration is convenient—is addressed by the bill's own design, which allows voluntary arbitration after a dispute arises, so only the take-it-or-leave-it pre-dispute clause is eliminated.

outcome.mechanism: It passed the House with every Democrat and one Republican in favor, then was referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee, where it never got a hearing or a vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Introduced in February 2021, it gathered 203 cosponsors — 202 Democrats and 1 Republican [S6].
The House Judiciary Committee reported it 23-14 in March 2022 [S7].

On March 17, 2022, a Republican motion to send it back to committee failed 208-222, and final passage passed 222-209, with all 221 voting Democrats in favor and only 1 of 211 voting Republicans [S8][S9].
Four days later the Senate received the bill and referred it to the Judiciary Committee, which took no further action through the end of the Congress on January 3, 2023 [S7].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers, banks, and other companies that use pre-dispute arbitration clauses keep the ability to route disputes to private arbitration and block class actions, and the arbitration industry keeps its contractual caseload. Consumers and workers with small-dollar and discrimination claims remain without a day in court.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Companies using forced arbitration and arbitration providers

for.role: House Judiciary Committee member; bill sponsor
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and steered it through committee to House passage.

for.name: 221 of 221 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Voted for final passage 222-209 and against the Republican motion to recommit.

against.name: Senate Judiciary Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never reported the bill
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on March 21, 2022 and took no markup, hearing, or vote for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: 209 of 211 House Republicans
against.what_they_did: Voted no on final passage and for the motion to recommit the bill to committee.

sides.party_line_note: In the House, all 221 voting Democrats voted yes and 209 of 211 voting Republicans voted no; the single Republican yes vote was the only crossover on passage [S9].

industries.industry: Arbitration providers and private dispute-resolution firms
industries.note: Their caseload comes almost entirely from pre-dispute clauses baked into employment and consumer contracts; the bill eliminates those mandates while leaving voluntary arbitration in place. Arbitration's advantage to companies is that a private, company-chosen forum hears each dispute alone, with limited evidence and little appeal.

Pre-dispute arbitration clauses and class-action waivers are the primary legal shield against wage-theft, discrimination, and harassment suits, including collective actions under wage-and-hour law; the bill removes that shield for future disputes.

industries.industry: Banks, credit card issuers, and consumer finance
industries.note: Consumer arbitration clauses block most class actions over fees, collections, and credit practices; the bill lets cardholders and borrowers sue in court and band together, restoring the class action as the main check on small-dollar consumer harm.

industries.industry: Nursing homes and long-term care operators
industries.note: Admission agreements routinely require arbitration of neglect and injury claims by residents and families; the bill would void those clauses for the covered civil rights and consumer disputes.
